passage:
During chemistry, Dorje checked his phone under the desk again: 212 likes yesterday, 148 now. His stomach dropped. Madhuri leaned over from the next bench. “You look like you failed a test.”
“Likes are down. I need something bolder.” He had already posted the neon-dyed hair photo, then a pouting close-up he didn't even like, and each time the number jumped, he felt light for an hour. Then it dipped, and he felt heavy again. All day his mood moved with a counter he couldn't control. At lunch he opened the app twelve times. Madhuri said quietly, “You were happier when you posted the picture of your dog.” Dorje shrugged, but he put the phone face down for the rest of the lesson.

qa.q: How many likes did Dorje's post have yesterday, and how many now?
qa.a: It had 212 likes yesterday and 148 now.

qa.q: How is Dorje feeling as the likes drop?
qa.a: Dorje feels anxious and heavy, since his stomach dropped and his mood moves with the counter.

qa.q: What could Dorje try instead of chasing bolder pictures?
qa.a: Dorje could post what he enjoys, like the picture of his dog, and check less often, since his mood should not depend on numbers he cannot control.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see Dorje's chasing of likes?
qa.a: Madhuri seems concerned but gentle, since Madhuri remembers when Dorje looked happier and says so quietly.

grounding: A teen posts bolder pictures to gain followers, feels anxious when likes drop and finds his mood tied to numbers he does not control.

passage:
Dear Parul Didi,
You asked why I deleted my account. I'll tell you properly.
In the summer I wanted followers. I had 180, and a boy in my class had 3,000 from doing stunts. So I started posting stunts too: a backflip off the park bench, then off the wall by the water tank, each one a bit higher, because the higher ones got more likes.
And I got hooked on the number. If a video got 400 likes, I felt great. If the next got 90, I felt awful all evening, refreshing and refreshing. My whole mood depended on people I don't even know.
Then in August I slipped on the wall and landed badly on my wrist. Papa found the videos while we waited at the clinic. He wasn't angry, just scared, and that scared me. We sat together that night and I deleted the account.
My wrist is fine now. My head feels quieter too.
Uday

qa.q: How many followers did Uday have at the start of the summer?
How did Uday feel when a video got only 90 likes?
qa.a: Uday felt awful all evening, anxious and refreshing again and again.

qa.q: What could Uday have done instead of chasing likes?
qa.a: Posted for friends Uday actually knows, and tried backflips only with a trained coach, so neither mood nor safety depended on strangers.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt finding the videos at the clinic?
qa.a: Papa was scared more than angry, realising how much risk Uday had been taking for likes.

grounding: Shows a teen posting ever more daring stunt videos to gain followers, feeling anxious when likes drop, and finding that mood rides on numbers nobody can control.

passage:
Jagdish, you asked why I went quiet online. I'm Chaitanya, and it's a bit embarrassing.
Last year I started chasing followers. I noticed my photos near the edge of the old fort wall got far more likes than normal ones. So every weekend I went back and posted something more daring: sitting on the edge, then standing, then one foot out for the camera.
The numbers became everything. A good post, and I'd be happy all day. A flop, and I'd feel sick, checking every five minutes, wondering what was wrong with me. I didn't control those numbers, but they controlled me.
It stopped when a guard at the fort caught me on the wall, pulled me down, and phoned my mother right there. She came straight away. She didn't shout. She just held on to my arm the whole way home.
I deleted those photos that night. I still post sometimes. Just not for the numbers.

qa.q: Who pulled Chaitanya down from the wall?
How did Chaitanya feel when a post flopped?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt sick and anxious, checking every five minutes and wondering what was wrong.

qa.q: What else could Chaitanya focus on instead of likes?
qa.a: Posting things Chaitanya enjoys for friends who matter, with fort photos taken safely from the path.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya's mother have felt holding that arm all the way home?
qa.a: She was likely frightened and shaken, relieved Chaitanya was safe and scared by how close it had come.

grounding: Shows a teen posting ever more daring photos to gain followers, feeling anxious when likes drop, and finding that mood rides on numbers nobody controls.
